stories.title: Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling

Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling. Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal Under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. stories.title: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes
stories.summary: A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation “Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes. The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material. Continue reading...

stories.title: Danny Kelly obituary
stories.summary: Ebullient journalist, magazine editor and broadcaster whose passion for music and football shone through all his work Danny Kelly, who has died aged 69, influenced music journalism and sports broadcasting for more than four decades. Humour, enthusiasm and encyclopedic knowledge were the hallmarks of his work as a writer and editor at the New Musical Express (NME) and Q magazine, and throughout his online, TV and audio career, most prominently around his passion for football. In 1997 Kelly helped set up Football 365, one of the earliest football websites, and still one of the most popular in the UK. He hosted radio shows on BBC 5 Live, TalkSport, BT Sport and Times Radio, as well as many podcasts including The View from the Lane, about the team he had supported since childhood, Tottenham Hotspur. stories.title: Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable
stories.summary: The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments. There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. The meek nature of Scotland’s collapse in the 4-0 loss to a second-string Switzerland was lamentable. The Belgian’s assessment, with overpraise a key theme, raised eyebrows. Continue reading...

stories.title: Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson
stories.summary: In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers Sign up for our free newsletter here Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling. This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Have a question for Jonathan? stories.title: ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future
stories.summary: At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’ After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.” In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. items.title: Fifa accused of climate ‘record of failure’ due to Aramco deal and tournament expansion
items.summary: Groups question ‘sincerity’ to meet emissions pledges Oil giant is a major sponsor of football governing body The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action. Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”. Continue reading...

items.summary: In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group. As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. This time around it would be the Australians that were to be the subject of a first-half onslaught, as a Jordan team inspired by Musa al-Taamari launched forward with wicked pace and ruthless intent whenever the opportunity, or space left by the Socceroo defence, presented itself. items.title: Do good club managers necessarily make good international managers? | Jonathan Wilson
items.summary: In a mailbag edition of our newsletter, we look at Mauricio Pochettino, Pep Guardiola’s international credentials and the lack of elite English managers Sign up for our free newsletter here Who should replace Mauricio Pochettino as the USMNT manager? – Tom S Although the salary I’m sure will be excellent, I think the US job is going to be a really difficult sell to a top-level coach. The 2030 World Cup is a long way away and I’m not sure the Concacaf Nations League, the Gold Cup or even the 2028 Copa América carry much appeal for a manager with European experience or aspirations. But I’m not entirely sure that sort of coach is necessarily a great idea. The last two World Cups, after all, have been won by low-key coaches who have come from within the federation and have worked with many of the players at youth level. That’s the positive from appointing from within; appointing from without is almost certainly more expensive and there’s the danger the next foreign manager does just what Mauricio Pochettino does, and has his head turned by the first vaguely attractive European job that comes calling. This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Have a question for Jonathan? items.title: Danny Kelly obituary
items.summary: Ebullient journalist, magazine editor and broadcaster whose passion for music and football shone through all his work Danny Kelly, who has died aged 69, influenced music journalism and sports broadcasting for more than four decades. Humour, enthusiasm and encyclopedic knowledge were the hallmarks of his work as a writer and editor at the New Musical Express (NME) and Q magazine, and throughout his online, TV and audio career, most prominently around his passion for football. In 1997 Kelly helped set up Football 365, one of the earliest football websites, and still one of the most popular in the UK. He hosted radio shows on BBC 5 Live, TalkSport, BT Sport and Times Radio, as well as many podcasts including The View from the Lane, about the team he had supported since childhood, Tottenham Hotspur. items.title: Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable
items.summary: The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments. There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. The meek nature of Scotland’s collapse in the 4-0 loss to a second-string Switzerland was lamentable. The Belgian’s assessment, with overpraise a key theme, raised eyebrows. Continue reading...

items.title: WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?
items.summary: Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. items.title: Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling
items.summary: Midfielder’s under-21s winner eclipsed Jude Bellingham’s mark and there was other talent to admire against France There may have been an Mbappé on the pitch – Ethan, the younger brother of Kylian, with whom he shares a near-identical gait – but by the end there was only one precocious talent on the lips of those watching England overcome France in their under-21s clash. Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling. Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal Under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. This time last year, after taking to the field at Slavia Prague aged 15 and 308 days , Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the Champions League. In March, six months on from his professional debut, he became the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer . He is the youngest player to earn a Premier League winner’s medal. Last month he was presented with three Guinness World Records. Continue reading...

items.title: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes
items.summary: A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation “Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes. The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material. Continue reading...

items.title: Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid
items.summary: ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards. items.title: ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future
items.summary: At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’ After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.” In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money. items.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
items.summary: The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona. Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.” Continue reading...
